#3337. Pokémon Colosseum Is Officially Coming To Nintendo Switch 2

Over the years, Game Freak has brought Pokémon fans all kinds of different games in the franchise, from sprawling open-world adventures all the way back to the original raft of Game Boy releases that started the whole journey. Along the way, there have been some arrivals that are markedly different from just about anything else.

Pokémon Pokopia is a solid recent example, applying the cute creatures we all know so well to a survival crafting formula. Back in the day, though, the examples that spring to mind most readily would be Pokémon Stadium and Pokémon Colosseum, both of which had been relegated to the annuls of time for the last couple of decades.

Pokémon Stadium has been available to Nintendo Switch 2 players for a while now, but Colosseum has remained noticeably absent, despite being the better game in the eyes of many. That was scheduled to change, but things have gone frighteningly quiet, leaving many wondering what exactly is going on.

In case you missed it, Nintendo announced a bunch of iconic GameCube titles would be coming to the Nintendo Switch as part of the Classics Catalogue (as long as you have the Expansion Pack). Those included games like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, F-Zero GX, and SoulCalibur 2, as well as Super Mario Sunshine, Fire Emblem: Path of Radiance, Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness, Super Mario Striker, Chibi-Robo!, and, crucially, Pokémon Colosseum.

The interesting thing about that is that all of those titles are now available for Nintendo Switch 2 players to enjoy, apart from the conspicuously absent Pokémon Colosseum. Neither Nintendo nor The Pokémon Company have commented on the reason why, though the length of the gap between the initial announcement and its still pending arrival would suggest that there may be some kind of issue.

As much as it's hardly the very best of the series to date, it really was a lot of fun to play back then, and returning to it in the cold light of 2026 would likely be a nostalgic experience, if nothing else. It would also come along at the perfect time, as the vast excitement around the 30th anniversary starts to die down and we wait to see what's coming next for the series.

What we do know in that regard so far is that the first games of the tenth generation will be Pokémon Winds and Waves. Within those, players will be exploring an archipelago of sorts, based on certain portions of South-East Asia.

As with all games that debut a new generation, we'll have a whole fresh roster of 'mons to track down and add to our dex. The last couple of generations haven't really managed to be as memorable as they were likely intending, so they could really do with a set of releases that managed to nail down a handful of iconic designs.

The next Pokémon games could also do with more than a subtle evolution in terms of the gameplay as well, with the last few efforts feeling like they were treading water more than anything else. If they can get it all right though, the games easily have the potential to recapture the magic of those first few iconic releases.

#3336. The Apple Watch's New 'Siri Recap' Feature Is Even Creepier Than I Expected

The “Siri Recap” feature that Apple announced in September is finally available in a developer beta, and I’ve spent the last 24 hours with the feature turned on. It’s even more unsettling than the “Live Rewind” feature that launched at the same time. It listens to all my conversations, and produces summaries that are both helpful and deeply creepy.

I have a button in the watch’s Control Center that can turn the recapping abilities off, but if I forget to do so, Siri listens to everything. I’ll get a recap of my entire evening, presented in roughly hour-long chunks, including things I would have completely forgotten I had even heard about.

The recaps somberly mention silly memes my kids were laughing about, and make major bullet points out of offhand remarks from brief conversations. If a conversation sticks to a single topic, I’ll often get a reasonably good summary of it, with specific facts and numbers highlighted; but just as often, Siri will get confused and mix up several topics or completely mishear a name or phrase.

Apple has four features that it considers part of “audio intelligence":

Music recognition, better known as Shazam. We’ve had a version of this on the Apple Watch for a long time now, although it has some improvements and now identifies music automatically.

Sound recognition, which can notify you about doorbells and babies crying. A version of this launched in 2020 as an accessibility feature.

Live Rewind, which gives you an on-wrist transcript of the last 15 seconds of detected speech.

Siri Recaps, which summarizes entire conversations for you to read on your phone.

Live Rewind had the flashiest demo from the Apple event: A server rattled off the day’s specials at a restaurant, and then the Apple Watch-wearing diner checked his watch to see a readout of exactly which dishes had just been mentioned. The utility is both obvious and kind of unnecessary: Why wouldn’t you just ask the server to repeat the list while they’re standing right there?

I haven’t found myself using Live Rewind, except out of curiosity about how the feature works. I discovered that it doesn’t pick up song lyrics very well, and also that by the time I think to check what was just said in a conversation, more than 15 seconds has passed since the part I was unsure about. I haven’t yet found a reason to use it for real.

But Siri Recaps? Those are both useful and unsettling. I enabled the feature, and decided to test it out later. But since it was on, it dutifully listened in as I picked up my son from school and gave him an update on an ailing family member’s health. We stopped by the library, and along the way we chatted about a variety of things: holiday travel plans, library policies, and the possibility of humans living in space in the future. Siri was listening to it all.

At least for now, the feature is only available in a developer beta, so sign up for that now if you want to try it. You'll need an Apple Watch Series 12 (or Ultra 4) and an iPhone 16 or better, excluding the 16e. (I have a 16 Pro, so I'm good.)

After you're updated to 27.3, go into the Watch app, tap Siri, and turn on Siri Recap. You can set a schedule for when it should listen (for example, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., if you want it on for the work day but off for the evening). You'll need to set a passcode on your watch, and you'll be guided through a step to upgrade your audio connection. The control center on the watch will have a button you can use to turn Siri recaps on and off at will. To read your recaps, go to the Siri app on your phone.

But still: I feel weird publishing the contents of these recaps, because they do contain things that people said to me in what they assumed was a private setting. I had the feature on when I attended a choir practice, and Siri recapped the brief chats I had with other choir members before and after practice. (Interestingly, it did not recap any of the quiet conversations I had with fellow sopranos while the tenors were rehearsing their part. I’m not sure if the watch was unable to hear us over the music, or if Siri is programmed not to listen when music is being played.)

Because speakers aren’t identified, it seems Siri doesn’t know what to do when there is a disagreement. A human note-taker would jot down that Person A made a point in favor of something, and person B made a point against. But when my son and I disagreed about how likely space colonization might be in the future, the recap didn’t reflect the separate positions that were put forth. It summarized the conversation as including “debating the feasibility and timeline of human space colonization and asteroid mining,” which isn’t exactly accurate, but close enough.

When it comes to the content of the discussion, the recap notes a bullet point of “skepticism regarding permanent space colonies within the next 100 years.” It didn’t include my reasons for being skeptical, and didn’t mention my son’s opposing viewpoint at all. If I were using this recap to jog my memory of the conversation, it wouldn’t be all that helpful.

Details are sometimes egregiously incorrect. After a discussion about a family member’s health, the recap had notes on the prognosis of “father.” The family member we discussed is not anybody’s father. Names in general seem to be a problem; I recommended a book to my son, and the recap includes notes about the content of the book, but not its title. The book’s author appears in the introduction to the recap (sort of a summary of a summary), but not in the content of the recap itself where the book is mentioned.

I should probably turn Siri recaps off. It seems wrong to let people chat with me without letting them know that their conversation is being ... well, not technically recorded, but basically recorded.

But it’s so tempting to leave it on so that I can review my day. Some of the details in the recaps are useful, like the dates that were discussed as options for a holiday party. The recaps will be deleted in about a week (unless I save them to the notes app), so if I want to remind myself of a conversation a few days ago, I should be able to scroll back through my recaps and find it.

I would be a fool to rely on the recaps, though. The most important points of a conversation are often left out; Siri doesn’t know what’s actually important, and there’s no way to guide it as to what to pay attention to. Specific details can be wrong, as I mentioned. There’s also no way to control when a “conversation” starts or stops, unless you are turning the recap feature on and off from the watch.

And there’s more: Not only are names usually omitted (wait, who did she say I should ask about that project?), the few identifiers that make it into the recap, like names of events, are often wrong. Subjects of discussion are often conflated in really unhelpful ways: My husband mentioned paying for certain course registrations for one of our children, and later I talked to that child about an unrelated exam. The recap got all of these things mixed up with each other and was wrong about pretty much every detail. About all the recap could usefully do is to remind me that something about AP U.S. History was discussed. Reading the recaps can be like reliving your day entirely in the passive voice.

#3335. iPhone is the winner of new battery test, topping all Androids

Last week CNET published an extensive battery test and the iPhone came out on top. But it wasn’t just one iPhone model that performed well, as several iPhones topped CNET’s list.

CNET pitted 32 modern smartphones against each other to see how battery life compared.

The winner? iPhone 18 Pro Max, which was followed closely by two other iPhone models.

Here’s the top 10 list, which contains several ties:

The 18 Pro Max has won the camera test, battery life test, and speed test over the top Android flagships. Other phones and Foldables might get more hype but when it comes time to perform head to head...the iPhone Pro Max comes out on top and we have video proof

As you can see, iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro both tied for second place alongside a pair of Android models. iPhone 18 Pro Max was the sole model that beat every other.

Each battery test is going to be a bit different, so results may vary depending on how you stress-test a phone. That said, here’s the method behind CNET’s test:

Each phone was put through a 3-hour streaming video test and a 45-minute anecdotal stress test, both with the battery at 100%. The results show the remaining battery percentage – the higher, the better. We averaged the results to determine our rankings

CNET says that in the 45-minute stress test they “stream videos, make a video call, play games and scroll social media.” So it’s an attempt at replicating normal use.

What’s your takeaway from the battery test results? Let us know in the comments.

#3334. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3333. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3328. Brand New Day Was Great, But Marvel Still Hasn't Done 1 Thing With Tom Holland's Spider-Man

As impeccable as Spider-Man: Brand New Day is, there’s still one thing the Marvel Cinematic Universe hasn’t achieved with Tom Holland’s Web-Head. Tom Holland's Spider-Man has undergone one of the most interesting journeys in the MCU timeline. Introduced as an enthusiastic teenager desperate to prove himself, Peter Parker has gradually become a more experienced, emotionally complex crime fighter. His story has also been closely connected to some of the MCU's biggest events.

Holland's natural charisma, excellent comedic timing, and ability to convey Peter's insecurities have made him one of Marvel's most consistently entertaining leads. More importantly, the character has finally reached a point where the consequences of his decisions can meaningfully shape his future, rather than simply serving as another stepping stone towards becoming an Avenger.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is an exciting new chapter in that development. Director Destin Daniel Cretton’s thrilling blockbuster allows Holland plenty of opportunities to explore a different side of Peter Parker, while maintaining the spectacular action and humor audiences expect. It is arguably the strongest installment of Holland's Spider-Man series so far. However, despite its success, Marvel still needs to explore one particular direction if it wants to get the absolute best out of its web-slinger.

One of the defining characteristics of Holland's Spider-Man has been his relationship with the wider MCU. Unlike Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield's interpretations, who largely operated independently of other superheroes, Holland's Peter Parker was introduced as part of an already-established superhero community. His first appearance in Captain America: Civil War established his connection to Tony Stark, with the billionaire becoming Peter's mentor throughout Spider-Man: Homecoming and Avengers: Infinity War.

Tony's influence provided an interesting alternative to the traditional Uncle Ben relationship, allowing Marvel to explore Peter's desire for approval from somebody he considered a genuine hero. However, it also meant that Peter's introduction to superhero life was heavily dependent on another character.

Spider-Man: Far From Home brought Nick Fury into the story, while Spider-Man: No Way Home featured Doctor Strange and a swathe of legacy Spider-Man characters. It was an enormously entertaining cinematic event, but it also meant that Holland's third solo movie was arguably his least independent adventure.

Brand New Day continues the tradition, albeit with a different assortment of familiar faces. Frank Castle, AKA the Punisher, is an important part of Peter's latest adventure, while Mark Ruffalo returns as Bruce Banner and Florence Pugh appears as Yelena Belova. These characters certainly have defined narrative purposes beyond simply showing up for the sake of recognition.

Nevertheless, the pattern is difficult to ignore. Across four solo movies, Holland's Spider-Man has shared significant screen time with numerous established characters. While he's garnered might be an impressive collection of guest appearances, it’s hard not to wonder if Spider-Man will ever get a truly solo adventure.

Importantly, this isn't necessarily a criticism of Brand New Day. If anything, Destin Daniel Cretton's movie proves that Marvel can incorporate its wider universe without allowing established characters to overwhelm the story. It certainly makes considerably better use of its supporting superheroes than No Way Home, which occasionally struggled to balance its emotional narrative with the excitement of bringing together so many familiar faces.

The difference is that Brand New Day has a much clearer understanding of what Peter's story needs. Following the events of No Way Home, everybody has forgotten Peter Parker exists, leaving him without the relationships that previously defined his life. His isolation is central to the narrative, and Holland gets plenty of opportunities to explore the emotional consequences of sacrificing his personal happiness to protect the people he loves.

That makes the inclusion of the Punisher particularly effective. Rather than introducing Frank Castle simply because audiences recognize Jon Bernthal's character, the narrative establishes an entertaining dynamic between two fundamentally different approaches to superheroism.

Bruce Banner's inclusion in Brand New Day is similarly appropriate, with Peter experiencing changes to his physiology. Banner's scientific knowledge and personal experience with an uncontrollable alter ego make him a logical person to consult. Yelena's appearance is comparatively brief, but Florence Pugh brings plenty of personality to her scenes without demanding that the movie divert attention towards the wider MCU.

The important distinction is that these characters contribute to Peter's development rather than simply reminding audiences that they're watching another installment of a larger franchise. Despite its extensive supporting cast, the most compelling material involves Peter, MJ, and Ned.

There's no reason Marvel needs to abandon crossovers altogether. The interconnected nature of the MCU is one of its greatest strengths, and Spider-Man's comic-book history is filled with memorable team-ups involving other superheroes. Peter Parker has fought alongside the Avengers, teamed up with Daredevil, and developed friendships with characters occupying completely different corners of the Marvel universe.

Those relationships are worth exploring, but they shouldn't be an obligatory feature of every solo adventure. The ending of No Way Home created an especially interesting opportunity to change direction with Peter is now completely alone, without Tony Stark's technological resources, the Avengers' support network, or even his closest friends knowing who he is.

That opens the door to a more grounded story built around Peter, a compelling villain, and the people closest to him. Rather than another world-threatening crisis, Marvel could explore the pressures of balancing superhero responsibilities with Peter's ordinary life, with several quintessential aspects still missing.

The Daily Bugle, J. Jonah Jameson, the citizens of Queens, and the neighborhoods Peter regularly protects are all essential parts of Spider-Man's identity. His relationships with MJ and Ned, meanwhile, offer a particularly rich source of drama following the events of No Way Home. There's plenty to explore without needing to introduce another superhero to explain the stakes.

Brand New Day proves that Holland can carry a compelling Spider-Man story while sharing the screen with other MCU characters. His next challenge should be doing so without them. Marvel has spent four movies establishing Spider-Man's place in its interconnected universe; now it should give him the freedom to occupy his own corner of it.

#3327. watchOS 27.3: Three new features coming soon to Apple Watch

watchOS 27.3 will launch to all users next month and introduce these three new Apple Watch features.

Siri AI keeps getting new features and also expanding to more languages. And in watchOS 27.3, the assistant will improve in both categories.

watchOS 27.3 upgrades Siri AI with new app actions across built-in apps like Calendar, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, and Weather. With these capabilities, Siri on your wrist can do more than ever.

There are also four new Siri AI languages supported in watchOS 27.3: Chinese (traditional), Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

For the latest Apple Watch models, watchOS 27.3 adds a new Audio Intelligence feature called Live Rewind. Per Apple’s website:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

I’m curious to see how useful this proves in everyday life. When Apple demoed the feature in September, it showed Live Rewind being used at a restaurant when an Apple Watch user missed part of the server’s menu explanation. Asking the server to repeat what they said seems like an easier solution, but perhaps there are other occasions Live Rewind will come in handy.

It won’t be for everyone, but I’ve been testing watchOS 27.3’s new Siri Recap feature and really love it.

Siri Recap only works on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and it’s off by default. But if you have one of those models and enable the feature, Siri can create automatic logs of what’s happening in your day-to-day life.

Most of the time, you won’t need to reference any of the recaps and they’ll be automatically deleted after a week. But based on my experience with the feature, Siri Recap definitely comes in handy at times when trying to remember key details from conversations.

Which of watchOS 27.3’s new features are you most interested in? Let us know in the comments.

Google’s Gemini AI chatbot app for Apple CarPlay is now available. The company confirmed that it is bringing the full Gemini Live conversation experience to CarPlay on Wednesday, and the app update arrived on Thursday.

Google bringing Gemini to CarPlay is especially notable for one reason. Gemini was the last major AI chatbot holdout.

CarPlay has supported AI chatbot apps and other conversational apps for a while now.

iPhone apps including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Copilot, Meta AI, and Grok all shipped CarPlay support already. Siri includes a standalone app in iOS 27, which also supports CarPlay.

Google has previously supported Gemini features through Google Maps on CarPlay, but not the Gemini Live experience through the dedicated chatbot app.

“Gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally starting today to all Gemini users on iOS across every supported Gemini Live language,” Google says.

“To get started, make sure you’ve updated to the latest version of the Gemini app on your iPhone, enabled microphone permissions, and used Gemini Live on your phone at least once. #3322. Nicholas Hoult’s New Heist Thriller Almost Had a Much Darker Ending

When it comes to the action-comedy genre, few directors are as accomplished and inventive as David Leitch. The former stunt performer/coordinator-turned-filmmaker returns with another high-octane action-comedy, How to Rob a Bank, which releases only in theaters this weekend. The director of thrilling romps such as Deadpool 2, Bullet Train, and The Fall Guy brings an extra punch this outing, as How to Rob a Bank tackles pressing and topical issues dominating the national discourse, particularly the wealth gap and the health care crisis. The 2026 film, starring Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Pete Davidson, and John C. Reilly, was screened as part of Collider's Screening series, with a Q&A featuring Leitch and his wife and producing partner Kelly McCormick, moderated by Steve Weintraub.

After the screening of How to Rob a Bank, Leitch and McCormick discussed their long creative partnership and the challenges they faced while filming their latest project, as well as getting candid about the state of America's political revolution in the wake of the recent midterm elections. The two reflect on the most difficult stunts they've pulled off throughout their career in Hollywood, with Leitch discussing his time as a co-director of the original John Wick. Leitch and McCormick share the creative process behind How to Rob a Bank, working on a constrained budget, obtaining music rights, blending crowd-pleasing entertainment with biting social commentary, and the film's alternate ending.

Below is a full transcript of the conversation between Leitch, McCormick, and Weintraub, with the full video of the Q&A available above.

STEVEN WEINTRAUB: For people that have not seen The Fall Guy, do you want them watching the extended cut or the theatrical cut?

DAVID LEITCH: I actually ended up liking the theatrical cut. I'm that rare director that goes through the process, and then realizes, “You know what? This is actually the best version of the movie, and most people will enjoy it.” When I sit back and watch the extended cut, it's like, oh, there's a lot of unicorns that we're missing! I don’t think you can go wrong with more unicorns. I enjoy them both, but I do like the theatrical [cut].

Going back into your stunt career. What's a stunt performed where you look back now and think “I cannot believe I did that?”

LEITCH: There was a time on The Bourne Ultimatum, and it's not the one you're thinking of. There was an explosion in The Bourne Ultimatum, where I'm standing in front of a car and it's like ten feet away. We were on some really long telephoto lenses, so everything feels compressed. I’m at a safe distance, and I'm hooked up to this wire rig, and you're just facing the car, and I literally just got off a plane that day because Dan Bradley [stunt coordinator] had called me to come in and double. I walk onto set, I go through makeup, and I stand in front of this thing that's all rigged. I haven't met this effects crew. It was one of those things where you don't have control over it–you're a passenger, and you haven't seen rehearsals. When I think of that, sometimes you have trust in all the people that make movies, but sometimes it's like as a stunt performer, you have to have a lot of trust. Watching that thing blow up, I'm like, “God, I hope the ratchet takes me away.” And it all worked out, but it was one of those ones where you're like, “Yeah, I signed up for this. That was a bad idea.”

So you spent a lot of time doing stunts and working with a lot of gifted filmmakers. I'm just curious, was there one or two things on a movie set that you sort of said, “I'm stealing this”? This is something that you now use on a daily basis or some lesson that you have applied to your own life from those early days working on all those sets.

LEITCH: There's a ton that gets absorbed. I don't have a lot of specifics that rush to mind, but there's one phrase that [James] Mangold gave me when we were working together on the first Wolverine. He knew I was aspiring to direct, and we had a lot of conversations about directing while I was on that film. I shot a lot of second unit on the first Wolverine. He always said, “You know what? It’s really important to cast the man. Cast the man. If they're halfway to the character already, you're golden.” I thought that was really smart. I think you look at your actors and if you can see something in them, that they could personify that character. There's something in their personality that you think they could pull out and make bigger. It is a good rule of thumb: Cast the man or the woman.

I definitely want to touch on Atomic Blonde just real quick. The stairway sequence [is something] people still reference and still talk about. For people that aren't familiar with what really went into that sequence, talk a little bit about how daunting that thing was from a producer standpoint. Did you ever think, “we can’t do this based on our schedule or budget.” What was it like behind the scenes putting it together?

LEITCH: Well, it was actually the opposite in the sense that it was a really small budget movie. Kelly, being the incredible producer that she is, challenged me and she said, “Look, you need to find some distinctive action. You need to figure out what's the moment in this film that makes it stand above all these small-budget action films.” In the past, we’d choreographed oners [shots in one take] and presented them to directors and it. You thought it was logistically hard, but it was really a challenge. I think we went to the stunt team and, ironically, Sam Hargrave, who was the second unit director and stunt coordinator on that.

He was like, “No, we'll never. It's going to be too hard. The actors will never be able to do it, and it's going to be these long takes. I don't want to do this. We're not going to be able to pull it off in the amount of time we have. It's going to take too much training,” and I'm like, “You guys will figure it out.” The choreography team went after it. Kelly and I went in and made a lot of adjustments. And then I had a great production team. Jonathan Sela, who really understood how we could light it and shoot it, and we put together a really amazing sequence for not a lot of money in Budapest. I think it was seven days for that sequence, all in with the car into the water. He didn’t want to do oners, and now that’s his thing. You see the Extraction movies, and the opening scenes are like 30 minutes long.

What do you wish more people knew about being a producer and being a director in Hollywood? I think a lot of people would like to do what you're doing, and what do you maybe wish more people knew or anything you want to share?

KELLY McCORMICK: I don't think anybody wants to be a producer! [Laughs] I don't think I wish anybody anything, to be honest. I do think that one of the things that I do as a producer is that I’m film forward. I can sort of navigate the studios needs, the director's needs, and everybody else's needs based on what the movie needs, if that makes sense. My goal is always everybody signing on to be making the same movie for a moment, go and really sussing out if people aren't on the same page about that as early as possible, to try to get people to understand the movie that we're all making, and then once you do that, then the film will tell us what it needs. We make a lot of different types of things. Movies need a lot of different things, different sizes, budgets, different directors. David's movies are all different in a sense. Following the film as the North Star is one of the things that I do that I think is specifically how I explain the job.

LEITCH: I think that's right, because I think producing is a title that can encapsulate a lot of different things, and everybody makes it their own and can make it their own profession in a way. Kelly has a unique way of working with multiple filmmakers, working with different size budgets, building a company, and then also managing our big films together. There are very few producers in Hollywood that have the ability to do that. Being in the business for 30 years, I haven't seen a producer that's that flexible.

LEITCH: Being a director is awesome. You get to have all these great artists working for you and you get to take their ideas and curate something great. I think the best part about it is being able to create art, entertain people, and then also start a conversation and I hope that's what we did with this film. This was really exciting for me to have this conversation that we're all having in America right now, and we had last Tuesday [Midterm Elections], and it feels like people want change, and so the challenge for me was like, “how can I embed that conversation in a fun action movie?” As a director, I get to do that stuff. I get to take on that challenge and make the art that I find interesting, and then you guys get to take it, enjoy it, comment on it, and go have conversations about it.

McCORMICK: I will say, on hard days, David's like, “okay, you know, do I get a decision today?” It's usually him really handling everyone else's needs the whole day and like trying to get his manipulating everything into what he needs as well.

LEITCH: Yeah, directing is the art of compromise as well. It totally is. You have a vision for something, and it's like a bag of marbles that you hold at the beginning of the day, and they just dump them on the table, and then the rest of the day, you're trying to keep all the marbles. That's directing really, essentially.

Kelly, I am a huge Weezer fan, and you are producing something called The Weezer Movie. What the f is The Weezer Movie?

McCORMICK: I cannot speak about The Weezer Movie! [Laughs] Not really. If you know Weezer, you know the movie is going to be very “Weezer-y.”

McCORMICK: I hope it's aiming for next year, Steven.

What's been the most difficult sequence of your career, and how close did it come to being like, “we can't do this?”

LEITCH: There were a lot of those on The Fall Guy. There were just a lot of practical stunts in that film. We were challenging ourselves to do them for real. We took a lot of time and a lot of prep to get it right. The car jump was scary in the sense that you were making that land on the ground. We were landing it ramp to ramp, but then when you actually put it up two stories in the air and do the same jump, you're just kind of like, “oh.”

McCORMICK: They were testing it near where we were shooting. There was this ramp to ramp, and they kept getting the ramps higher and farther apart as they succeeded every day, basically. The set was actually manmade, but it was also filled with dirt and stuff, and I was just really worried that the wind, the rain, or even the sun would be pushing one side or the other differently than we were expecting. It needed to be exact. I made them do that survey that they do on the streets all the time. Every day, I was like, “Do the survey; just tell me that it's not eroding leading up to it." The crazy part with that stunt was that it was really the speedometer that ended up being problematic. It tripped up and stopped working while he was taking the ramp. It was very programmed exactly how fast he had to go in order to make sure he got to the other side ,and it was wrong, and he was slow, and he felt it, and he punched it, and he got over. In the movie, you can see it.

LEITCH: He clipped the front of it and he hit more of the set than the ramp.

McCORMICK: You can see the set just flying in the movie. That's him barely making the ramp. That one was really intense. That one's one where, if it goes sideways, it's not a good thing. Honestly, some of How to Rob a Bank was stuff that I was like, “Are we going to be able to get it done?” David puts 800 pounds of genius and a 2 pound bag, like no matter what size he's doing. And in this case, it was a modest budget. The needs were still really high. It was all of our guys who worked on, three times, four times the size budget that this was. The film is shot on 35 millimeter, and then on Prosumer, and at the end, it's on digital. There are only 230 extras, which is for the riot, which is like not a lot considering what we're doing. They came up with the most genius ways of stacking the extras. If you saw the shot where John is racing and trying to get to Nick, that's like the way that they shot it, made it look like there were tons of people. There were not tons of people! Some of the scariest parts to me is not being able to have the resources. Weirdly, that's scarier than a stunt to me.

I actually have a question about that. You mentioned you have a limited amount of extras. With the way technology is now, how much do you think about [not using AI], but using technology like CGI to add more people in or do you want real people?

McCORMICK: I mean, it depends on the movie, probably.

LIETCH: CGI wouldn't have looked great, you know. The top shot, at the end, where we crane up, it's the drone shot where Nick is laying out on the pavement. I'll be honest, I added a few people in CGI because we had less extras, and so we made it look like there was more of a group, and CGI worked great there.

McCORMICK: By the way, this movie couldn't afford much CGI either.

You guys are offered a whole bunch of stuff at this point. What was it about this one that said, “We have to do this”?

LEITCH: The script really spoke to us. What's been going on in the last couple of years and reading this script, it just felt really timely and really relevant. Actually, we passed on it, because of the size, and we were going to look and go into some bigger things, and we just couldn't let it go. A couple weeks later, we reengaged and said, “you know, we really want to do that.” Again, I really wanted to just address the elephant in the room. We have this massive disparity of wealth with young and old. Could I tell that story and be part of the conversation using sort of the 87 North Engin–the David Leitch engine–of action and comedy, and be a little bit more message forward than I normally am, but also make it an entertaining ride and have people enjoy it, but then at the end of it, feel something and maybe there's a call to action for you in your own life to do something for your neighbor or go out and vote and hold your politicians accountable. This originally was going to come out on Labor Day, and I think Amazon had wished for it to go out on Labor Day, and I think the timing wasn't right for marketing, and we found a great slot at the end of the year or so. Every week it gets more timely. It's not like the movie's lost its timeliness. After Tuesday, it’s even more timely. That was the goal with this film. It was to do something provocative and dangerous, but also entertaining.

McCORMICK: It's a subject we're really passionate about, and we wanted to use our platform to join the conversation and to be part of it like a [time] capsule film. There were two other aspects that were really exciting to us. I think David always bends genres or at least adds to the conversation of the genre, and heist movies aren't like this movie, right? The robbers are hiding. They're not trying to hide in plain sight. The message is so forward in this movie in the coolest way that’s almost done with this bravado that they're going to get away with it. It's so Gen Z in that way. They do it for longer than they probably even think, but it's worth it for the message because they're that devoted to what they want people to hear. To try to make change, which was what was cool about it. The second part was to try to find a way to connect with social media and creator storytelling in an authentic way. Everybody’s watching. These creators have such connectivity to their followers. What's the difference? How can you play in both formats? How do they meet? Where do they meet? How do they connect? How do they answer and question each other? We thought that that would be a really fun opportunity for David to play in that space. I haven't really seen a movie that does it in the same way, and I think it's one of the achievements of the film.

I really love the way you did the YouTube stuff with Nick talking to the camera. Talk a little bit about putting together those YouTube clips, because they're very effective and they're dropping truth bombs on the audience. You’re not lying with these numbers.

LEITCH: No, not at all. I think that was one of the fascinating things about the script initially. You read those first numbers. Then you do a little research and you're like, “wow, really?” I think people will be shocked by it. It’s a real motivation to want to rob a bank. The first video was scripted, and there were other videos along the way, but they were really more like The Anarchist Handbook. It was very grounded. Social media doesn't feel like that to me. I mean, the things that I watch are really entertaining and they're engaging and they're crazy. I started to rework those sequences and created the persona of The Wolf that wasn't in the script. We created the gang wearing these colorful masks. The whole social media thing became its own life in the pre-production process. I started to write those edutainment videos so I could drop them in at different places in the scripts to carry the story forward, but also keep the energy going and, again, combine these two storytelling styles. You see in the middle of the second act when they get caught and there's the interrogation scene, those two styles come together, and that's where life really meets social media. Nick is breaking the fourth wall on film, and we're using graphics over film and there's a song playing like you would [hear] if you were watching a YouTube thing, but it's like carrying you through the whole piece. That was an intentional thing. How can we, like Kelly said, bring these to make a modern piece about social media and its power? It’s still grounded in these people's real traumas that have led them to wanting to rob banks.

I know you guys made this on a budget, so how the f did you get Radiohead and Billie Eilish? You have some real needle drops in this movie, and they're big songs.

LEITCH: Kelly is always good with me at the beginning when there's a budget and we're looking at line items and you look at your spreadsheet. You realize, “How much am I going to need for Dave’s musical appetite?” We usually set that aside, and it's like, “Wait, that's two days of shooting?!” But we do it because I know it's going to make the film. I know for me, as a storyteller, that's an emotional cheat code. It's shameless, but it's premeditated. I go through the script and there are needle drops that come to mind, and 99% of them stick. And then I formulate my shot sequences around that music. That sequence in the interrogation scene, I knew we were going to use Lily Allen and we were going to use “Fuck You.” I'm shooting it in that way. It’s shot to the music and we know how we're going to edit it. At the end of the movie, with the Billie Eilish song, that did change. That was Lewis Capaldi for the longest time. It used to be “Someone You Loved,” which is also beautiful. We changed it at the last minute, but I still shot that section like a musical piece intentionally.

McCORMICK: We loved it so much, and then it was exactly what happened with the playability of that song. Everybody overplayed it, and so did we. Young women actually were testing really high in the film, and they would literally write like, “is there any way to change out that Lewis Capaldi [song]?” They're our biggest lovers of the movie. We got to take care of the ladies!

Billie Eilish works pretty well. Radiohead is pretty selective with what they allow. How tough was it to actually get “Karma Police”?

McCORMICK: We work with this music supervisor named Susan Kent, and she's really awesome. I don't know how she gets the deals that she gets. I just say, “is there any way to get it lower?” And then she says, “yes!” There are times where we write love letters. David wrote a love letter to Billie Eilish. I think you wrote something to [Radiohead] as well. We show them clips of the movie sometimes to show them where it's going to play, which works really well for our films because it's usually a pretty good use, and that sometimes brings the budgets down, but it also just gets you the song sometimes, too.

LEITCH: You know, people believe in it. I think this was a special piece where they knew the material. This movie has a little bit of a message.

McCORMICK: The Billie Eilish [song] I learned is a toxic breakup song. I thought there was something so cool about it in the sense that it's kind of a toxic breakup from the system. We added that component to it, even though it is kind of their love story. At the same time, there's such sorrow to it that I think it kind of works for everything you need to feel.

This isn't really a question. It's more like a statement. I just want to make sure I say out loud that the health insurance industry in America is out to fuck you, and anything that we can do, especially in your movie to get more people talking about this, is very important. That's all I got. I give credit to Amazon for being behind it. It's a huge corporation pointing out some of the bullshit.

McCORMICK: Everybody inside of Amazon is really passionate about the movie. They were so incredibly supportive. You've seen the work that they're doing on social media, especially. These trailers are out of this world, and you could just feel that this is hitting us all, even when you're working there too, you know? It’s pretty interesting to see how much everybody who's been a part of it galvanized around it. One of my favorite stories [was] when we were shooting in the streets of Pittsburgh. If you've ever shot with extras, you know that they barely stick around for lunch, let alone stick around for the full day, let alone if you're shooting nights. They don’t stay all night or come back the next night, forget about that. We shot two weeks of nights in downtown Pittsburgh, and every night there were five more people! They came, and then they brought five friends, and we ran out of masks, costumes, and everything, because it just became this movement in Pittsburgh while we were shooting it. They all came to party. It was like a rave. They made their own signs. It was just so cool and it made us feel like this is what we want people to feel coming out of the movie, too. You don't have to riot, per se, or rob a bank, but together you're stronger. Find your communities, say your truth, let's make a change.

I need to talk about editing, because you guys know I'm fascinated by editing.

McCORMICK: Elisabet Ronaldsdottir crushed this.

LEITCH: The Icelandic genius. She edited the first John Wick and all of our films. She's amazing.

Everyone in this audience knows that I love John Wick. A lot of people don't remember that it was possibly going straight to DVD or straight to Blu-ray. I could be wrong about this, but then Lionsgate picked it up and then it became a thing.

McCORMICK: It’s more complicated, but we should talk about the editing on How to Rob a Bank.

What is it like when you guys are in the editing room and you're putting together the assembly cut, because you've worked on a number of movies. When you're making your assembly cut, which is where you take all the footage and put it together, have you ever wanted to, like, jump out the window when you have an assembly cut? Or do you always have something?

LEITCH: That's a great question, Steve. Wow. You should do this for a living! Sometimes, you see it, and you're like, “what have I done?” I hide it really well! I do try to walk in with positivity, but there are times where I'm like, “oh, my God!” I trust Elisabet, who's amazing, and I trust Kelly. Elisabet has seen a lot of material over the years, and she's really brutally honest, and she pulls no punches. She can look at you and go, “we have a great movie.” If she looks at me like, “we got some stuff to figure out,” and then I’m like, “oh shit, now we really got to go to work.” Post[-production] has become a passion for me. During the first Wick, I didn’t love it. I didn’t understand that letting go amplifies another scene, and as I’ve grown as a filmmaker, post has become one of my favorite places to play. We were meticulous about the editing in this film. We got to play with those video sequences that were edited in a different house, but then [they were] brought in and we re-edited them. Getting the timing just right, playing with the music, adjusting the sound, having a scene in, having a scene out, watching it again. I love that process. I've become really comfortable with letting things go to make for the greater good. I would be bad on an island where you have to pick somebody to go and be like, “it's the greater good. You got to go out.”

For people that don't realize how, how long does it typically take for you guys to edit a film? I don't think people realize that it’s a battle. You are working long hours for many months to put something together.

McCORMICK: We have a pretty short editing schedule. I think it's 27 or 28 weeks.

Tell the people, is that like a Monday through Friday? Is it 9 to 5?

LEITCH: Yeah. It's more like a 9 to 7. There’s a lot of things going on. You have your editor who's working on scenes you may be watching, you divide the movie into different reels so you can actually digest it in a way so that you're not rewatching everything all the time. I might be watching a reel doing notes, Elisabet might be working on a second reel. We may have an assistant editor looking for sound or a different take.

McCORMICK: You’re working with your composer, you're working with your visual effects team, you're having meetings all the time on iterations of either music or effects. It’s a lot.

LEITCH: It’s kind of endless. There's so much to do that the day just gets consumed.

McCORMICK: There’s a 10-week period that’s contractual with the DGA. I think people really think that that's a ton of time, and then they run out of time. That happens so often that they didn't have the discipline in those ten weeks, and things go off the rails because it feels like you've got all the time in the world, and then you are out of time so fast.

LEITCH: What I like to do now is to get my first six weeks. I'm super intense and I try to get to the strongest version of the movie that I'm feeling at the moment. I try to get a really strong assembly cut, reduce it down. I bring Kelly in for fresh eyes and then it's like dropping a hand grenade on it! “Damn it, it was good for a second!” Then I have another four weeks to take those ideas and shape them. The movie ultimately becomes better the more you put it under pressure.

McCORMICK: David's director's cuts are really mature, so it's nice, because then the studio can see what the movie is. You're basically testing that cut. He's pretty accepting of notes, if they’re really good, at the director’s cut phase, to do his first preview so that, again, we're making the same movie with the studio. It's not like a split where it's like it's his cut versus theirs. We've never really done that. Then it’s testing it again and really listening to the audience for confusion, for pacing, for jokes, for songs, and then finishing it, which takes forever, too, because it's like three weeks of mixing. It's the slowest process in our high-tech world to have AI taking over our jobs. They have to mix a reel and then match the reel to the edit, and the conforming. It takes forever. I go, “Isn’t there a way to do this faster?!”

LEITCH: You're sliding things around frame by frame to get the sound back to where it was when you make an edit.

McCORMICK: It’s like three weeks of that, going back and forth and then listening again and going back and forth, then it's color.

LEITCH: You can see how much Kelly loves post!

McCORMICK: I actually do! I like it more than production!

Every time I hear from people about what goes on behind the scenes, in terms of making some of these movies, and the bigger the film, the longer it can take and the more meticulous, it's crazy. What was the last thing you cut out before you picture-locked [on How to Rob a Bank]?

LEITCH: Let me say this, because I would be more like the last thing I put in because we were toying with the ending. If you were having the real feels when he's laying on the ground and the camera's moving up, we could have gone to black. That was my first ending of the movie, but I shot all the other endings.

LEITCH: It leaves a very, very different feel. I wanted this to be a call to action, and I wanted this to be about hope. At the end of the day, I thought it was better to go with the original ending that we shot. I kept watching the film, and I was really moved by that moment.

How did you decide on how to escape prison? When you do something like that, are you in the back of your mind, like, “well, we might want to continue the story”? Or is it like, “we're just going to have fun with this”?

McCORMICK: It actually stemmed from just wrapping, and the hope. Wrapping up Renzi, it worked so well that you knew that he was still doing stuff and like going to hack his way into some more fun videos, and it wrapped up Anna Sawai’s character so well, and then it gave you hope. It wasn't about a franchise play at all. It was just about hope in this case.

LEITCH: Exactly. It was really more of just wrapping up this movie, because I think it was really a one-off about this message.

The best movie title of 2027 is you guys. You own the best title of next year. They made another movie and the title is…

McCORMICK: It’s definitely a palate cleanser from tonight.

You've done a lot of second unit [directing]. How much do you lose your mind having a second unit director on your movie? Because I would imagine you want to shoot absolutely everything, or maybe I'm wrong about this.

LEITCH: I don’t have a lot of second units on my set. I don't push a lot off to the second unit. When I do, I generally have great people that I trust that have been with me for years. On this film, Greg Rementer directed all the heist stuff, and that was the stunt team dressed as the actors, because we're using masks. I just let them go wild.

McCORMICK: There were like a thousand cameras on everyone, prosumer cameras, the drones, and he shot them like they were a play.

LEITCH: We shot it like it was just real life. You're capturing it like a content creator would, right? There's just cameras everywhere, and you're seeing the cameras. There’s a lot of trust with me and the stunt teams, because we go way back, and I've been in that world for so long.

I could ask you guys a million other things, but I'm going to get killed. I've already gone way too far and so on. I'm just going to stop there and say, congrats on the movie.

LEITCH: You’re already going to get killed by the health insurance industry!

Fuck the health insurance industry! I hate them so much. No one should go bankrupt in America for having to go to the doctors.

#3321. Apple offers a military discount, here’s how to get it

If you’re a member of the U.S. military, Apple offers an easy way to save 10% on eligible products and accessories. It’s available to current and veteran members of the U.S. military and their immediate family members living in the same household. While you’ll need to verify your eligibility to access the discount, the process is simple. There are also a few limitations you’ll want to know about before placing an order. Here’s everything you need to know.

A 10% discount is available to current and Veteran members of the US Military, National Guard and Reserve. Immediate family members who reside in the same household are also eligible.

Verification is handled through ID.me. Creating an ID.me account is free, and current military members can verify their service using their .mil email address. Veterans can enter details of their service information for ID.me to verify, or upload images of official documents (such as a DD-214) for ID.me to review and confirm their eligibility. Once you’re verified, your ID.me account can also be used to access military discounts from other retailers and services that support ID.me verification.

Once verified, you can start shopping by visiting Apple’s Store for Veterans and Military. The discount only applies to Apple products and accessories (including Beats) so third-party products aren’t eligible. Apple services, such as Apple Music and iCloud+, are also excluded. Orders can be shipped directly to you, or you can choose in-store pickup if the product is available at a nearby Apple Store.

This is probably the biggest catch. Apple specifically says ACMI isn’t available when shopping through the Veterans and Military Store. You can still earn 3% back in Daily Cash with Apple Card, but you lose the option to finance your purchase at 0% interest over several months. Apple Upgrade also isn’t available when purchasing through the military store.

The only way to get the military discount is to make your purchase through Apple’s website in a browser. The Apple Store app isn’t an option, which means you also can’t take advantage of Apple’s “Get Ready” feature to select your iPhone model, color, storage capacity, and carrier ahead of pre-orders opening. Instead, you’ll have to navigate Apple’s website on launch day, when demand is high and server traffic can make checkout more challenging. Whether the 10% savings is worth giving up the convenience of a potentially quicker checkout is ultimately up to you.

The military discount can’t be combined with carrier promotions or discounts on iPhone purchases. You can still trade in your existing iPhone through Apple and receive the applicable trade-in value, but you can’t take advantage of carrier-specific trade-in offers, like promotions that give you a larger credit when you trade in an eligible device and activate or upgrade a line.

These purchase limits reset on January 1 each year.

Apple’s military discount is a useful perk, especially if you’re buying a product at launch and want to save 10% right away. However, it’s worth comparing prices with other retailers before you buy, since sales and promotions can sometimes beat Apple’s discount. The military store also comes with a few limitations, so you’ll want to weigh the savings against the features and payment options you’re giving up. Even with those caveats, 10% off can make a real difference on an expensive Apple purchase.

#3319. 8 Best Survival Drama Series Of All Time

The survival genre has produced many great shows, often with a sci-fi or action bent. Lost might have been about a group of castaways on the surface, but it soon became much less straightforward — the show needed extra explainers because the Lost timeline became so confusing. Regardless of sub-genre, though, all survival dramas are about characters doing their best to stay alive in circumstances they rarely, if ever, expected to find themselves in.

Many of the best survival dramas feature small groups of people suddenly forced to work together after disaster strikes, causing beliefs and personalities to clash. Others involve so many characters it’s hard to keep track of them all, with numerous conflicting factions springing up. Some begin immediately after the event that changes everything, while others start their stories years down the road. Whichever way a survival show structures its characters' challenges, there's something for everyone in TV's best survival dramas.

Very loosely based on a Belgian comic book series, Jeremiah aired on Showtime and starred Luke Perry and Malcolm-Jamal Warner. Set in 2021, the series follows two people living in a world where, 15 years earlier, a virus known as “The Big Death” wiped out almost everyone over the age of 13. The leads meet by chance when they’re imprisoned by a warlord and recruited by a guy to help a mysterious organization. Their journey leads them to discover Thunder Mountain and the Valhalla Sector, both organizations trying to rebuild the world in very different ways.

While some survival dramas focus on people's fight to stay alive, Jeremiah took a different approach. People had already learned to survive because it was set 15 years after a pandemic. This series was more concerned with what came next — the rebuilding of society and the new systems and institutions that underpin it. It also explored what kinds of communities would spring up in a new world originally led by children. It was somewhat hopeful for such a depressing premise, though; Jeremiah wasn’t so much about what was lost, but about what humanity could do better the second time around.

AMC’s The Terror is an anthology series that explores real-life historical events through a fictional (and supernatural-tinged) lens. The Terror season 1 follows the doomed crews of HMS Terror and HMS Erebus as the ships become stuck in the ice while trying to make their way through the Northwest Passage in the Arctic Ocean. Based on a book inspired by the 1845 expedition led by Captain Sir John Franklin and Captain Francis Crozier, season 1 is a bleak, haunting look at men trying to survive in impossible conditions (while eventually being hunted by a monster).

Watching these sailors try to stay alive in a land of nothing more than snow and ice is harrowing, and not surprisingly, some of the men turn to cannibalism. However, while the harsh conditions might be most likely to kill them, they aren’t the only threat to survival; violence between the factions that occurs in the crew also springs up and leads to some pretty gruesome moments. The Terror season 1 isn’t for those who enjoy people actually surviving in survival dramas, as there’s little hope.

When Netflix released The Society, critics praised it for its social commentary and storytelling. However, the show only lasted one season; the second season was canceled during the COVID-19 pandemic. Unfortunately, that means there’s no resolution, but The Society is still one of the better survival dramas around. When a group of teens returns home from a school trip to find that every adult in their town has disappeared — and they’re now mysteriously cut off from the rest of the world — they have to learn to survive on their own.

Thankfully, these kids aren’t starting totally from scratch. They have resources, and they end up creating a society based on communal living. However, teenagers will be teenagers, and it isn’t long before power struggles, hormones, and total anarchy threaten the tenuous situation. The mystery of what put them in this scenario in the first place adds an extra layer of depth to the story. Lord of the Flies was a major influence, but it was also compared to The Leftovers and Lost.

Imagine growing up on a space station because the planet your people originated from suffered a nuclear apocalypse a hundred years ago, only to be thrown back down to that planet with 99 other juvenile prisoners to see if it's habitable once again. That was the premise of The 100, a survival drama that saw a group of teens forced to learn how to survive in a place they never could have imagined.

As if finding food and resources wasn’t hard enough, the group eventually learns that people survived the dangerous radiation levels all those years ago, so the planet is actually inhabited. Though The 100 had its moments of controversy and flaws, it also featured all the hardship and drama expected in a survival show. Each season turned into a different kind of fight to keep living; it became a story about how far people will go to survive.

The Walking Dead began as a comic book series, became a hit television show, and then branched into numerous spin-offs, creating a monster franchise. While it’s a horror show about zombies, its main premise is the survival of those who weren’t immediately killed or turned in the initial outbreak. During its long run, the show evolved from following the original group of survivors as they learned to exist in this new world to different human factions rising and clashing.

The Walking Dead franchise has expanded far past the original show, and this means that there is more than one way for viewers to watch the series.

It’s one of the ultimate survival shows, and while it went off the rails at times, it showed how great the human spirit can be in the face of adversity (even if that adversity is the walking dead). The series also proved that when the world as we know it ends, humanity is the scariest monster around.

Before Yellowjackets, there was The Wilds, a survival drama about a group of teen girls on their way to an empowerment retreat whose plane crashes, leaving them stranded on an island. The girls must learn to work together to survive and find a way off the island — only, as it turns out, they’re actually unwitting participants in a social experiment, so getting off the island will be harder than expected.

The second season adds a group of teen boys to the mix, as their plane also crashed on the island as part of the experiment. This brings even more tension and terrifying drama. Featuring flashbacks and flash-forwards, The Wilds explores how surviving an ordeal like this can change a person and who they become when it's all said and done.

When it comes to survival dramas, there are few better than Lost. A plane crashing into a mysterious island and a group of survivors working together to get off that island is the epitome of survival setups. The introduction of the polar bears, the Smoke Monster, the Others, and so much more allowed the show to develop a rich mythology and added an edge to the group's survival story, turning it into one of the most popular TV shows ever made.

While survival shows existed before Lost, this series set the blueprint for many shows that followed. With glimpses into the past and future, Lost turned this survival story into a deeply emotional, highly philosophical saga that still resonates with viewers.

Yellowjackets is one of the most recent offerings in the survival drama genre, and to say it's made a splash would be an understatement. Like Lost, the show starts as a fairly straightforward story about a girls’ soccer team whose plane crashes in the wilds of Canada. However, as the series goes on, things take a dark turn, and something supernatural constantly lurks in the background.

The showrunners wanted to explore how trauma can shape lives and interpersonal dynamics within social hierarchies, and they managed to do that with Yellowjackets. Those eventually rescued from their plight were drastically changed by what they experienced. The cannibalism and ritualistic elements give the show a horror edge as well. The final season premieres on November 20, 2026. It's time to find out how Yellowjackets ends.

#3318. iCloud+ has new perk in iOS 27 if you pay for more storage

The tentpole feature of iCloud+ is cloud storage, but Apple keeps improving and expanding the service to include other perks too. And in iOS 27, iCloud+ has a new benefit for high-storage tiers: AI features for HomeKit cameras.

With iOS 27, iCloud+ has added a new perk if you pay for more storage: Apple Intelligence features for compatible Home cameras. Per Apple’s website:

With Apple Intelligence in the Home app, you can automatically generate video descriptions for recorded clips from compatible Home cameras. You can then search your recordings using natural language

These AI-generated video descriptions provide a convenient summary of what’s happening in your home, let you browse important clips at a glance, and search the camera’s recent history of recordings.

The price ladder requirement for the 12TB plan in order to get 5 cameras is WAY TOO HIGH. I rather dedicate a local mac running some sort of AI model that can do this locally instead of paying that.

All of this is available with a camera that supports HomeKit Secure Video (I recommend this Aqara camera for $35). But because AI features depend on Private Cloud Compute, Apple only offers them on the following iCloud+ plans:
