SATURDAY AM: Paramount is still looking at a $20M opening for the Johnny Depp comeback movie, Ebenezer, but rivals see it lower. The hope is that families show up today as we hear the Ti West genre fans didn’t come out in droves last night; Friday and previews at $6.7M. One indication that it’s appealing to families is that the AMC Disney Springs is the pic’s highest grossing location with close to $25K so far.

Other good news is that the movie is playing evenly throughout the country: East, South, Midwest, South Central, and Mountain. You never want a movie that just plays on the coasts. PLFs are accounting for 36% of the gross. CinemaScore is great A- with a 65% definite recommend which is alright on Screen Engine/Rentrak’s PostTrak, which could mean a slow burn. Diversity demos show 48% Caucasian, good 28% Latino and Hispanic turnout, with 12% Black and 6% Asian American. Big chuck is older skewing with 37% over 45 while the 18-34 set is 40%. Overall, the pic is leaning 52% female, with women over 25 the biggest demo at 41%, which is not surprising on a Depp movie.

Columbia Pictures and Mandalay’s action-thriller Ghost Soldier posted $1.55M on Friday from 2,558 locations for a $4.9M 3-day and $8M five-day. The core audience likes it at 90%, they just didn’t show up in droves. The pic at net $18M, co-financed by TSG is cheaper than Amazon MGM Studio’s How to Rob a Bank which cost $40M before P&A. Older audience here at 49% over 45 with 57% guys and 55% Caucasian, 22% Latino and Hispanic, 14% Black, and 4% Asian American. Pic is playing best in South and South Central where close to 40% of the gross is coming from versus a norm of 27% for other movies in the marketplace. The Harkins Estrella Falls 16 in Arizona is the leading single-location with $4K since Friday.

The David Leitch directed action movie How to Rob a Bank needs to rob more to pump up its gross after a $2.2M Friday/preview for what looks to be a $4.7M opening. CinemaScore is a B-, which is lower than Leitch’s last movie, The Fall Guy, which landed an A-. Male leaning at 57%, with the 18-34 demo at 66%. Men over 25 were the biggest at 37%, followed by women over 25 at 28% and then men under 25 at 21%. The movie needed more of the latter to show up to make this work. Caucasians are 42%, Latino and Hispanic at 26%, Black at 15%, and Asian American at 9%. PLFs repping around 27% of the weekend so far. AMC Waterfront 22 in Pennsylvania is the top grossing venue with $13K.

It’s a low weekend at the box office with around $80M for all movies, though interestingly enough, it’s +8% from a year ago when Lionsgate’s Now You See Me: Now You Don’t opened to $21M. It feels like this is the calm before next weekend’s storm, which will be Lionsgate’s The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping which many believe has a shot to open at $100M.

We’ll have more updates and the chart for you later this morning.

#3274. Robert Christgau and Carola Dibbell Talk New Documentary ‘The Last Critic’ and Staying Crazy in Love

The Last Critic is one of the year’s most fascinating rock documentaries — even though it’s not about a musician. It’s a portrait of the legendary writer Robert Christgau, the self-proclaimed “Dean of American Rock Critics.” He was one of the pioneers who invented pop-music criticism in the Sixties — but six decades later, at 83, he’s still at the top of the game. He began his Consumer Guide column in the Village Voice in 1969, and has kept cranking it out ever since, now on Substack. For generations of music fanatics, Christgau’s voice hits like Bob Dylan or Neil Young — two artists his age who are still doing it with the same fiercely independent spirit he brings to his writing.

The debut feature from director Matty Wishnow, The Last Critic won the jury prize at the South by Southwest and Oak Cliff Film festivals, as well as the 2026 Screen Dallas grand prize. It gets its New York premiere tomorrow. The film, which is co-produced by longtime Rolling Stone contributor and editor Joe Levy, goes beyond music, because it’s also the portrait of a marriage. Christgau and his wife, novelist Carola Dibbell, have been together more than 50 years. Over the decades, they’ve shared an intellectual life, raised their daughter, collected way too much vinyl, and — the weirdest part — remained crazy in love.

Christgau has a fearsome rep for never pulling his punches, with his own savage wit. Lou Reed spent a chunk of his live album Take No Prisoners complaining about getting a B+ grade for Street Hassle; when U2 won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 1988 for The Joshua Tree, Bono jokily groused in his speech about his band’s reviews in the Village Voice. Christgau’s inspired more songs attacking him than any other journalist, from Sonic Youth (“Kill Yr Idols”) to Public Enemy (“Bring the Noise”).

But there’s something obsessive about his lifelong quest to chronicle the music, still going strong after 60 years — he’s heard more albums than anyone on the planet. When he reviewed Prince’s Dirty Mind in 1980, he dropped one of the most-quoted one-liners in critical history: “Mick Jagger can fold up his penis and go home.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

The Last Critic features artists Christgau has reviewed, as well as writers he’s inspired, from Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore to Pulitzer-winning novelist Colson Whitehead. (I make an appearance as well.) There’s a touching interlude with his lifelong friend Greil Marcus, the only other OG rock critic who’s kept doing it this long (or this well). In one of the most surprising moments, the legendary songwriter Randy Newman recalls their friendship, and admits he wrote a song about Christgau and Dibbell, “Lost Without You,” inspired by the closeness of their marriage. It’s the kind of movie where you come for the rock, stay for the romance.

Rolling Stone met up with the couple at the same East Village pad they’ve called home for 50 years. The place is packed with albums, books, art — the first thing that greets you at the door is a painting of the Shirelles. They talked about the doc, seeing their marriage up on the big screen, the art of arguing, playing hoops with Randy Newman, and the strange college semester when Christgau was Gene Simmons’ professor.

Congratulations on the movie.Robert Christgau: It came out really well. When [director] Matty [Wishlow] called me up and asked if I would do it, the first thing I said was, “Yes, if you include my marriage,” which at the time I think took him aback. However, he came to feel that it was the marriage that made the movie, which is what I believe.

It is the marriage that makes the movie.Carola Dibbell: But it’s still about you. I’m a co-star. Related Content Andrew Watt on His Insane 2026:  Madonna, McCartney, the Stones, Gaga  The Rolling Stones' Release Date for ‘Foreign Tongues’ Deluxe Edition Look for the Legends in the Best Rock Album Race at 2027 Grammys Alexander Skarsgård Embraces His Magnetism in the Rolling Stones’ Video for ‘Mr. Charm’

When I first saw it, I told the director, “This is a love story. A very strange love story.”Christgau: Well, I agree. I think that’s the best thing about the movie. The relationship really has a kind of vitality to it that you can see. And that’s exactly how I feel about Carola, and that’s the most important thing in my life. And it’s really nice that it actually comes through in the imagery of the film. I think that’s the reason people like the movie, too.

When did you two get together?Dibbell: The summer of 1972. Bob and I had known each other. He was my friend Dominique’s boyfriend. Bob had had his eye on me all this time, but I was just so delighted to have him as a friend. I knew that he was a rock critic, but I really was not like a groupie. I met him in the summer of 1970 — we were all having breakfast at Ratner’s Deli. But I then got into an argument with you about Godard.

Christgau: She knew more about film than I did.

Dibbell: Bob and I had a big argument about it, but then we became friends anyway, and then he began to date Dominique, and so we just knew each other. But eventually, everything changed for me.

Christgau: I’m so glad it did, Carola. She was an incredibly cute woman with a Radcliffe degree.

Dibbell: The thing is we were both English majors. One night we were playing a party game called “Celebrity,” and we needed to come up with a celebrity whose initials were an M and a C. And we both came up with Martin Chuzzlewit [the title character in an 1844 Dickens novel].

Now that’s two people destined to be together. I think that’s why people respond seeing such an unusual couple onscreen.Christgau: What makes it so unusual?

Two people, very extreme personalities, who stay madly in love for 50 years of marriage, but remain individuals in a totally unfiltered way.Christgau: I don’t know how extreme I think we are, but—

Dibbell: Really? I really don’t know that, but I believe you.

You both make a strong impression. Let me put it that way.Dibbell: Well, at the time that we got together, it was … I’m not going to say “turning point,” but it was sort of a point where one chapter in the counterculture and the movement was easing into another. People were asking, “Oh, is it OK to be a feminist and get married?” Bob was a feminist too, and he always liked smart women. And so we both were trying to figure out, how do you do this? A marriage of equals?

Something I love about the documentary is how it captures your enthusiasm for the art of a good argument. Dibbell: I used to say that if I told him “I agree with you,” he’d say, “That’s where you’re wrong.” He just couldn’t stop arguing.

Dibbell: Yeah, you. Who do you think we’re talking about? But it just comes very easily to both of us.

Would it be fair to say that you both have argumentative personalities?Christgau: I don’t think Carola has an argumentative personality.

Dibbell: There’s where I disagree with you.

I guess I mean a “debate” more than an “argument.”Dibbell: I think I argue more than I debate, actually. But it definitely improves our thought to be arguing together.

Christgau: I got Carola to start writing rock criticism, not because she was my wife and I wanted to give her the work — although, obviously, that was part of it. But because A, I knew she could really write, and B, she had knowledge of the subject.

Dibbell: I found rock criticism so interesting as a form, being a writer, and I was very interested in the unreliable narrator and all that kind of thing. Then when I read Lester Bangs, I said, “Oh, yeah! Why not be literally ambitious while writing about this declassé music stuff?”

Christgau: He could also write a paragraph in about a minute and a half.

When you began writing in the Sixties, there wasn’t a lot of serious attention paid to pop music.Christgau: But Rolling Stone was doing that a lot. Rolling Stone was a crucial part of why all of that happened. Jann Wenner had a head for finding the most interesting writers, many from the Boston college scene, and that was a really important factor in why I got to do what I did. No question about it.

And also the fact that I was already friends with Greil Marcus. That was a crucial part of it as well. He was at Rolling Stone, and frankly, I think he had Jann Wenner around his little finger. Because Jann was smart enough to know that this guy was really something else.

Early on, you wrote that your biggest influences were Thelonius Monk and Alan Freed.Christgau: Let me tell you, Monk has lasted. I still play a lot of Thelonious Monk. Carola gets a little tired of it.

Dibbell: I finally say, “Can we listen to The Clash?”

But you always had an appreciation for AM radio. You were open to tawdry pop trash.Christgau: It wasn’t “tawdry.” Come on.

You were writing in the Seventies about how great KC and the Sunshine Band were. In the Village Voice.Christgau: It’s all well-made, that’s the thing. Extremely well-made. That proves my point.Dibbell: It proves your point.

Determined as you are to undermine the entire premise of my point, I’m going to make it anyway. When I first read your Consumer Guide as a kid in the Eighties, I couldn’t believe there was an adult writing about Funkadelic and the Go-Go’s and Donna Summer and A Flock of Seagulls and taking it seriously, as art.

Christgau: Four hours a day listening to AM radio had something to do with that. But I wanted to write about pop art as an important phenomenon.

There’s a great story in your memoir about when you were teaching the rock criticism class at CUNY on Staten Island in 1970, and one of your students was a kid named Gene Klein.Christgau: Who later became Gene Simmons.

I always wonder what the dragon from Kiss learned from you about music critics.

Christgau: He just sat in the back and kept his mouth shut.

Something The Last Critic documents is your insanely obsessive online following, around the world.Christgau: One thing that happens with this movie is people in Sweden and Norway coming up with their dog-eared copies of my books.

Dibbell: It was so funny hearing about Europeans with tattered versions of the first Consumer Guide book.

Christgau: So I had this fanbase all over the world, and I had no idea it was there, really. I was writing for the Village Voice, and they paid me decently, and I had a lot of autonomy, and I really valued it.  But when that ended, I kept writing. I managed to have a whole life as a critic, and it’s not like I’m working for Variety or the Times. I feel not just fortunate, I feel like I built something.

Dibbell: But there was a point when you were having conversations about whether you should stick with the Consumer Guide or whether you should write more essays. Also, I remember I had to argue Bob into writing the memoir, Going Into the City. You felt, “Why would anybody want to read my story?”

Christgau: Which came out pretty well, I think.

Dibbell: Yeah, it did. But you resisted that. Editors thought you should write more essays, but I felt that the Consumer Guide was such a great form that you shouldn’t stop doing it. And I also understood that you had a fanbase based on that. I wasn’t even thinking so you can make a living — but just with me, my constant struggle to get a book published, I just felt this is a great thing, that fanbase. You’re very lucky that people want to be your fan.

How did you become friends with Randy Newman? He plays such a surprising role in the movie. Dibbell: He was lovely.

Randy Newman talks about writing a beautiful love song about you two, “Lost Without You.”Christgau: I will say I was very proud. I wrote about Randy in the very beginning, and I felt that Randy really did understand that I got him. I was early on it. I was initially assigned by this guy from BMI named Russ Sanchez when I was writing for the BMI magazine who told me about this songwriter guy named Randy Newman who they wanted to have a piece on. At that time he lived in a house somewhere in the Valley, so I went there and I interviewed him. And then we went out to the ballpark and played basketball. This was a long time ago — I don’t play basketball anymore. But we had a game of basketball.

Dibbell: Don’t you each remember that the other one won?

Christgau: Well, he was taller than me. But I do rebound with a certain amount of verve.

It started with basketball, but how did that turn into a long-running friendship?Dibbell: He wrote you a fan letter in the Nineties, saying that he admired your perseverance, the way you kept up with new music, that it was something he did not actually understand, your enthusiasm for it. But he was interested in hip-hop and he wanted you to guide him. He wanted you to recommend him some hip-hop.

What did you play him?Dibbell: Public Enemy, I think.

Christgau: I’ve always had a high opinion of him.

Dibbell: We had lunch with him — this was in the old days when we had an answering machine. We got a message from someone claiming to be Randy Newman, and I said, “Oh, it’s not Randy Newman.” But you got back to him and said, “Was that you?” And he said, “Yes.” You were both old by then.

Christgau: We went to lunch. Then he came back to our place, even though he could hardly walk.

Dibbell: He had some bad knee problem, but you wanted to play him some new music. He climbed the stairs. Then he looked around our apartment, and he said, “If you wanted to fix this place up, I could loan you some money.”

He’s so sincere in this movie — we’ve never seen this side of him before. It’s probably the only Randy Newman song anyone would want to be about them.Christgau: Yeah, it’s a great compliment. I liked that song before I knew it was about us.

Were you surprised by The Last Critic, when you finally saw it?Christgau: I think a better way of putting it is that I was more pleased by it than I anticipated being. And I was especially happy about how important a role Carola played in it. Matty hadn’t made a movie before. This was not his area of expertise. But he ended up making a really good movie.

It just seemed like, “OK, you want to do this? What do you see in a documentary about a critic?”

But it goes beyond that. It’s the love story, in a collaborative life of the mind.Christgau: That is the thing that I like best about it, and I’m proud of it. Obviously, I’m very happy who it was a love story with. If it had been about [the legendary New Yorker and Village Voice journalist] Ellen Willis [his Sixties ex] and me, it wouldn’t have been this good. Ellen’s as smart as anybody I’ve ever met. But Ellen didn’t like music as much as Carola ended up doing. [Dibbell comes in from the next room.] I was just saying you were a better rock critic than Ellen Willis.

Dibbell: I respect her tremendously. Her work was foundational.

You were on the scene for so many pivotal rock moments, like the Monterey Pop festival and Woodstock. A fan on your Substack recently found a photo of you in the crowd at Monterey. Christgau: About the third row, yeah. Nobody at that time understood how important Monterey was going to turn out to be historically, as this event that really just pretended something was happening — but then it really happened. Woodstock itself was a strange and interesting experience, which involved a lot of lying around the grass, among other things.

The way you wrote about women musicians in the 1970s was very ahead of the curve culturally. You were engaging with feminist ideas at a time when it was rare in music journalism. There’s a really moving moment in the doc when the writer Jessica Hopper discusses reading your words on Joni Mitchell.Christgau: Let it be said that Ellen Willis was not without her presence in that fact, because Ellen Willis really made me a much more fervent and conscience-driven and militant feminist. It was really important to me to be a feminist critic. I mean, I had those impulses anyway, but Willis obviously solidified them, without any question. I’ve been writing about women making rock & roll since the beginning. Joy of Cooking and Fanny are bands that 90 percent of people have never heard of.

You were taking Dolly Parton seriously as a writer in the 1970s, when most of the media treated her as a joke.Christgau: But Patti Smith was out there covering “Jolene,” right? Glad she’s still around. How old is Patti?

Dibbell: She’s a little younger than us, but not that much younger than us. So, what, she’s in her seventies?

She turns 80 in December.Dibbell: And Debbie Harry? I think she’s older than me.

You had a great line about a Billy Joel album in the Eighties: “Sexual-politics rads like me were fretting about a decade ago come home to haunt guys who thought they were a crock.”Christgau: I said that? That’s pretty good. But as far as my marriage with Carola is concerned, one thing that’s really significant about how it happened is that I went out with one of her best friends, for close to a year before. And so Carola was someone I really knew fairly well, but it wasn’t like we were dating.

Dibbell: Not even a little bit. I was really not ready to get married again in that time. I’d been married before — I got married on my way to get divorced. I was not ready for a potential husband, so I was very happy to know Bob as a friend.

As you said before, you were figuring out a new way of doing this — a marriage of equals. Dibbell: Well, I had to figure out how to be heard, when you were surrounded by people who were just going to listen to you. I had to figure out how to do that. Despite all the struggling to be an equal and all that, I do spend a lot of time feeling like Bob is doing what he’s doing, and I’m helping make it work. But at the same time, I mean, when I finally published a novel [The Other Ones, in 2014] and had readings and did events as myself, it was very different. And Bob was great. He came as my date on an event I did at Rochester [New York]. He said “I love being the date. I love not having to do the work.”

Some of the best moments in the doc are just you two geeking out about music together.Christgau: There was an emotional weight to it that most documentaries about critics wouldn’t have. I just understood that the marriage was integral to the fact that I did this work, and therefore it had to be there.

Dibbell: I believe Bob when he says that, but I don’t necessarily experience it that way. I mean, I rarely talk you out of an opinion about a record.

Dibbell: I mean, I really was amazed by how much of this movie was about work, judgment, criticism. So there are all these shots where he’s writing at his computer, with all these piles of books collapsing around him. And he’s sitting there thinking, “Is this an A or an A-minus?” But one of my favorite scenes is when I’m editing Bob. Just because it seemed so relaxed and there were so many things we agreed about without really having to spell them out. And I like that. I like that a lot.

I’m just so used to this setup — our marriage, how we interact with each other — I don’t even think about how it works. There’s just so much that we share. I’m so used to it. Christgau: After half a century, I would hope you’re used to it.

#3273. Apple TV 4K review: The best streamer comes at a cost

It’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here. There’s Siri AI support, a faster chip, an improved remote, and more.

Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.

The Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged. It’s still the same familiar black box that sits underneath your television. The only visual change is that the front status light has moved from the right side to the center.

Inside, Apple has upgraded the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip, touting 50% faster CPU performance and twice the GPU performance.

Those are great improvements on paper. In practice, I’m not doing anything on my Apple TV that really stresses the performance. Compared to my third-generation Apple TV 4K, I’ve occasionally noticed slightly smoother animations and faster performance in apps that handle more processing locally, like Infuse.

I think the biggest advantage of the A19 chip is future-proofing. People tend to buy and keep these devices for years. In fact, I’m still using a first-generation Apple TV 4K from 2017 in my bedroom, and it still works just fine nearly a decade later. The A19 gives the new Apple TV plenty of performance headroom for future tvOS updates and more demanding apps, even if those advantages aren’t particularly noticeable today.

The Siri Remote looks the same as before, but it now supports Precision Finding in the Find My app, making it easier to track down when misplaced. You can also play a sound on the remote to help locate it. I lose my Siri Remote all the time, so this honestly might be the change I’ve noticed and appreciated most in my 10 days testing the new Apple TV.

It’s worth noting Apple also sells the new Siri Remote separately for $59, and it’s compatible with every previous Apple TV 4K generation. You do, however, need a newer iPhone model to use Precision Finding.

One of the more interesting new features is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room. Apple TV automatically calibrates the speakers based on their positions in the room.

For context, I typically use my Apple TV with a stereo pair of full-size HomePod (2nd generation) speakers. I’ve spent some time testing the new four-speaker surround sound setup by adding a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers.

My house’s layout isn’t particularly well-suited for a traditional surround sound setup, but to my admittedly untrained ears, this sounds great. I can’t speak to how it compares to a dedicated surround sound system, but I appreciate Apple continuing to expand what’s possible with HomePods and Apple TV.

One of the biggest changes with the new Apple TV 4K is the addition of three far-field microphones. This means you can now interact with Siri without picking up the Siri Remote. In conjunction with this, Siri AI is also coming to Apple TV.

Siri AI brings the same broad world knowledge and personal-context capabilities you’ve experienced on iPhone and HomeView, but adapts them to finding and watching content on your television. Siri AI on Apple TV requires the owner of your Apple Home setup to have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Personal context requests also require a paired compatible device connected to the same Wi-Fi network as Apple TV.

What was that TV show Lily recommended a few weeks ago?

What are some baseball movies I might like?

What did the vet say after Blake’s vet appointment?

For each example, tvOS responded with a dedicated interface on Apple TV, showing the answer along with poster art, cast information, and more. It also offers built-in contextual suggestions when you ask for recommendations, so you can refine the results further.

You can also ask Siri contextual questions about the show or movie you’re watching. This includes things like “where was this show filmed?” and “when is the next season coming out?”

I’ve found Siri AI’s responses to those contextual questions less accurate. It struggles to accurately identify the show or movie that’s playing, leading to completely inaccurate responses to those types of questions.

It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021 and the third-generation model from 2022. The far-field microphones are what’s exclusive to the new hardware. This lets you shout Siri commands into the air without talking directly into the Siri Remote.

In my testing, hands-free Siri works relatively well, and it’s convenient to control Apple TV without reaching for the remote. It does a good job at picking up commands

I can’t go any further in this review without talking about the price. The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) costs $299. That’s a huge increase over previous Apple TV models. Here’s a brief history of Apple TV 4K pricing over the years to set the stage:

After Apple introduced the $129 Apple TV model in October 2022, I started to notice a change. More and more people had Apple TVs when I would visit. Friends and family who had previously bought an Amazon or Roku box, or just used their TV’s built-in software, had purchased an Apple TV.

At $299, I worry that type of adoption is going to come to a screeching halt. And it’s unfortunate because the Apple TV is so much better than anything else out there. tvOS is fast, clean, and relatively free of the clutter and advertisements you find on competing platforms. The Siri Remote is excellent, and the integration with the rest of Apple’s ecosystem is hard to beat.

I could justify the $299 price for the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) if it were just one option available in a broader lineup. If there were lower-priced options for people who don’t need all the bells and whistles. That’s not the case, though. In fact, this is the first Apple TV 4K generation to be sold in just one configuration. There’s no cheaper version with less storage or fewer features.

To Apple’s credit, these are devices that can last for years. The fact that I’m still using an Apple TV 4K from 2017 makes the $299 price a tiny bit easier to swallow, but it doesn’t really change my frustration.

Apple seems serious about its new smart home strategy. There’s the HomeView smart display, a new HomePod mini, and the Apple Home Collection family of smart home accessories launching later this year. One of the best ways to get deeper into people’s homes is by controlling how they watch TV. I can’t help but think pricing the Apple TV 4K out of reach for so many people will hinder those ambitions.

Don’t get me wrong, I love the Apple TV. I have three of them in my house. If one of them broke, I would reluctantly pay $299 for a new one. Whether you fall into that category is for you to decide. All I can say is that the new Apple TV 4K is the best streamer on the market.

#3272. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

HomeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

HomeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

In terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-issue. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

In practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

HomeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could quickly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone users.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple says that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

The faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

There is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:

I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

However, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

One of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

HomeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

The feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

There are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

HomeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

The facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

In practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

HomeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

Siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

HomeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you currently can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software update coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for quickly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

When you get a new iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

HomeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

It’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

In fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

#3271. Billy Evans Claims He “Did Not Give Consent” For ‘You Can See Everything’ Nudity, Still Loves The Doc: “It’s Entertainment”

After finding out you really can see everything in A24’s Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim doc, Billy Evans is sharing his side of the story.

Elizabeth Holmes’ husband has recently given his first interview about You Can See Everything, claiming that he “did not give consent” to feature his full-frontal nudity in the documentary, which has sparked Oscar buzz since its premiere last month.

“Now, did I know they were filming me in the shower? Yes. But we would film 16 hours a day,” he explained on CBS Sunday Morning. “Like, all sorts of things were filmed with assurances made. I was just as surprised as the rest of the country to have my whole body on camera for the world to see, and it’s been an awkward experience in having, like, your kids’ teachers see that. It’s really uncomfortable.

A24 told CBS in a statement, “Everything that was filmed was filmed with their consent.” Watch on Deadline

Evans confessed “I love the film,” despite being made out as a villain. “I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it’s entertainment, you know, and I didn’t get to control that edit,” he said.

“I’m deeply passionate about my family and about the work that I do,” Evans said in the interview. “But no, I am not some controlling monster who’s leveraging his wife for insert-whatever-anybody-is-saying. No, I am not those things.”

The Haemanthus founded added of being villainized, “It’s super-painful, but me being angry about it doesn’t help change it. Look, I’m going to live my life with integrity and with who I am, and I hope people can see that over time. But if they don’t, what I care about is the people that I know, people that love me.”

Evans thinks A24 is “probably worried I’m gonna sue ’em” over his depiction, but he has no intention of taking legal action. “Because maybe I’m a different person than most people think I am,” he said.

In You Can See Everything, disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes invites Fielder into her and husband Billy Evans’ home to document everything in the month leading up to the start of her 11-year prison sentence on fraud charges.

#3270. Red Hot Chili Peppers Donned Their Bushiest Rick Rubin Beards for Wild Rock Hall Performance

The Red Hot Chili Peppers honored 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Musical Excellence Award recipient Rick Rubin by playing one of the biggest songs they made together, and dressing up like the legendary producer.

Taking the concept of “imitation is the sincerest form of flattery” to its funniest possible conclusion, all four members of RHCP took the stage at Saturday night’s Induction Ceremony in Los Angeles wearing ludicrously big, bushy white beards and wigs. They also all sported some very Rubin-esque orange-tinted sunglasses, while drummer Chad Smith played a special drum kit with a portrait of Rubin emblazoned on his bass drum.

For the performance, the Chili Peppers ripped through “Give It Away,” off 1991’s Blood Sugar Sex Magik, the first album Rubin produced for the band. (Since then, he’s produced all the band’s albums except 2016’s The Getaway, which Danger Mouse helmed.) Some technical difficulties with Flea’s bass caused an initial hiccup, but the band easily recovered after starting the song over, their fake beards bouncing wildly as they ran around the stage. #3269. Nintendo's Black Friday Deals Are Actually Pretty Good

Black Friday is nearly upon us. From now through Cyber Monday, retailers and companies alike are offering deals and discounts on their wares. While I always keep an eye out for Nintendo deals offered by stores like Amazon and Best Buy, it seems the company is offering its own discounts this year—and, surprisingly, they're actually pretty solid.

On Thursday, Nintendo announced its Black Friday discounts. We've already seen Switch 2 sales ahead of the Black Friday season, but now, Nintendo has confirmed an official discount for the console. Starting Nov. 22 through Dec. 5, you can pick up Nintendo's Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99, down $50 from $549.99. That includes the console, a download of Mario Kart World, and a 90-day Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

If you already have a Switch 2 console and/or Mario Kart World, you're not left out of the Black Friday deals here. From Nov. 22 through Nov. 29, Nintendo is also running discounts on several high-profile Switch and Switch 2 games. During this promotion, each of the following is $39.99:

Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2

Nintendo rarely offers official discounts on some of its biggest titles, especially in this current era. Games like Donkey Kong Bananza retail for upwards of $69.99, so you're saving as much as $30 on these games during this week-long promotion. In addition, Nintendo announced a sale on its digital store that runs from Nov. 19 through Dec. 2, though it didn't say which titles would be on sale. Just keep an eye on all these dates: The Switch 2 console promotion runs longer than the physical and digital games discounts, while the digital sale runs longer than the physical sale.

Nintendo says that these discounts will be available "at select retailers," as well as its brick-and-mortar locations in New York and San Francisco. You can also buy the Switch 2 bundle through Nintendo's website.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Use price tracking tools to determine if the deals you're keeping tabs on are actually a deal. If you feel like that's too much work, we already do that for you, so follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products makes you focus and make smarter decisions.

#3268. Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified

Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

#3266. David Tennant Teases “Very Small Part” In ‘Only Murders In The Building”, Addresses Future Of ‘Doctor Who’: “It Deserves To Run Forever”

David Tennant is in two Hulu series releasing in late 2026, Season 2 Part 2 of Disney+’s Rivals, which is now streaming, and Season 6 of Only Murders In the Building, which premieres December 8.

During an interview with Deadline breaking down this week’s eventful three-episode return of Rivals, Tennant spoke about doing the new season of Only Murders In the Building, which sees the crime-solving trio of Charles (Steve Martin), Oliver (Martin Short) and Mabel (Selena Gomez) traveling to London to solve the murder of true crime podcaster Cinda Canning (Tina Fey).

“I’m the the definition of a cameo. I think you may also call it a very small part, but it’s either a very small part or it’s a cameo, depending on how confident I’m feeling,” Tennant said. “But lovely to be part of that, and with those legends, what a treat! To go on set like that, something that’s so established, and with people who would have every right to be terribly grand and rather standoffish; to be able to delight in their company and to work opposite these people who you have admired for years, and to find them approachable and funny and great to work with, it’s a true pleasure.” Watch on Deadline

The Season 6 OMITB guest cast — a who’s who of British actors — includes three Doctor Who stars: Tennant, who played the Tenth Doctor and the Fourteenth Doctor, Jodie Whittaker, the first woman to portray the iconic Time Lord, and Peter Capaldi, who played the Twelfth Doctor. (Also recurring is Jim Broadbent, who played an alternate version of the Eleventh Doctor in the 1999 Comic Relief special Doctor Who: The Curse of Fatal Death.)

The iconic Doctor Who is going through a complete revamp, with the BBC evaluating bids for Season 16 as part of a competitive tender launched in September. The process involves a bake-off, in which producers are asked to pitch new takes that would keep the series “relevant, surprising, brave and inspiring for both long-standing fans and new audiences.”

Deadline asked Tennant, the actor probably most closely associated with the role of the Time Lord, whether he thinks the Doctor Who franchise will survive?

“It depends who gets it, doesn’t it, and what they do with it,” he said. “It’s clearly a format that has legs. It’s done all right to survive since 1963, so there’s every reason to believe that it can. I think it’s difficult for anything in the current environment, especially a show like that, which needs a bit of money behind it, and I don’t necessarily know where that will come from. I’m so outside that loop now because all the people that I do know are no longer part of it. So I guess it depends who wins the the tender.”

Deadline has revealed that Line of Duty showrunner Jed Mercurio and his Hat Trick Mercurio, STV Studios as well as likely two different BBC Studios labels are in the running, with the process still ongoing.

“I hope so,” Tennant said about Doctor Who continuing as we await the results. “I love it. It’s a true television original, and it deserves to run forever. It will in some form, the fandom will keep it alive. We’ll have to wait and see, I’m sure somebody brilliant will give it a go. So there’s no reason why not.”

#3265. Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony

Cynthia Erivo and Blink-182’s Travis Barker took the stage at the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony to pay tribute to one of this year’s honorees, Phil Collins.

Though the pairing of Erivo and Barker may seem unlikely on paper, it proved to be an inspired choice as they performed Collins’ timeless 1980 hit, “In the Air Tonight.” Erivo delivered the song with the perfect amount of drama and bravado, while Barker pummeled his kit with precision when it came time for that all-important drum fill.

Along with performing “In the Air Tonight,” Barker delivered Collin’s induction speech. He recalled the massive influence Collins had on him as a drummer and singer-songwriter, calling hits like “Sussudio,” “Take Me Home,” “Easy Lover,” and “Against All Odds” the “soundtrack to my childhood.” As for “In the Air Tonight,” Barker said the song had “arguably the most badass drum fill of all time. You don’t even have to be a drummer to know that fill. When that part comes on, everybody plays air drums.”

Inducted this year as a solo artist, Collins previously entered the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2010 as a member of Genesis. The musician declined the opportunity to perform himself, admitting in an interview earlier this year, that he wasn’t “match fit.” (Collins hasn’t played live since March 2022 and has faced several health challenges since then.) Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, and Gram Parsons received the Early Influence Award; Rick Rubin, Philly Soul songwriter Linda Creed, producer Arif Mardin, producer Jimmy Miller were honored with the Musical Excellence Award; and Ed Sullivan was given the Ahmet Ertegun Award.

#3264. 10 Shows Like 'The Traitors' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

What started as De Verraders way back in 2021 has become a global reality phenomenon: Peacock in the U.S. hosts the American version with the sartorially supreme Alan Cumming, and also the earlier UK take as well as iterations from Australia, Canada, and New Zealand—but there are spin-offs in France, India, Germany, Ireland, Turkey, and more. Basically, throw a dart at a map and you're likely to hit a country with its own take on The Traitors. And yet! The addictive nature of reality TV means that we can't really ever get enough. In that spirit, here's more backbiting reality TV, and a couple of dramas that offer up similarly duplicitous thrills.

A reality show with a complex history as relates to The Traitors, the premise being so similar that it may well have served as an inspiration. Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.

#3262. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3261. Top Wall Street analysts are confident about these 3 stocks for the long haul

Global stock markets have been under pressure as geopolitical tensions have resurfaced in the Middle East. Moreover, investors remain concerned about the sustainability of AI-driven demand and infrastructure spending.

Nonetheless, those looking for attractive stock picks amid the ongoing volatility can gain key insights by tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts. These experts assign ratings after in-depth analysis of a company's fundamentals, growth opportunities, and risks.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

E-commerce and cloud computing giant Amazon (AMZN) is this week's first pick. Heading into the company's second-quarter earnings, TD Cowen analyst John Blackledge reiterated a buy rating on AMZN stock, citing strength in the Amazon Web Services cloud unit as well as the e-commerce and advertising businesses. The analyst lowered his price target on AMZN stock to $340 from $350 as he revised his estimates and slightly raised his capex projections.

Specifically, Blackledge expects Amazon to report revenue of $200.1 billion, 2% above the Street's consensus, driven by acceleration in AWS and advertising revenue. He also expects the company's e-commerce business to reflect the shifting of Prime Day in the U.S. and other key markets to the second quarter this year, compared with third quarter of last year.

In particular, Blackledge expects AWS revenue to grow 35.5% year-over-year in Q2 2026, marking an acceleration from 28.4% in the prior-year quarter and 3.4% above the Street's expectations. The 5-star analyst expects revenue to be driven by rising generative AI workloads as the company's significant AI infrastructure spending helps to ease supply constraints.

Regarding third-quarter outlook, Blackledge said, "Our rev and Op Income estimates are 0.3% and 3.2% above consensus, driven by further AWS revenue growth acceleration led by AI demand."

Blackledge ranks No. 771 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 55% of the time, delivering an average return of 11.2%. See Amazon Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to semiconductor company Marvell Technology (MRVL). Following several meetings with management, RBC Capital analyst Srini Pajjuri reiterated a buy rating on MRVL stock with a price target of $360.

"Overall, the meetings reinforced our conviction that MRVL can sustain 40%+ growth for the next 3 years, driven by strong AI demand, optical connectivity leadership, and expanding Custom pipeline," said Pajjuri.

The 5-star analyst added that robust demand and limited supply are giving greater revenue visibility. Pajjuri noted that Marvell's data center business is on track to deliver more than 50% growth this year and next. Also, the growth in the company's networking business is outpacing compute, driven by agentic AI and inferencing workloads.

Meanwhile, Pajjuri noted that optical product lead times have extended to more than six months, while XPU customers are placing purchase orders 12 months in advance. While the analyst kept his estimates unchanged, he sees the possibility of upside for the second half of 2026 from the Optical business, with more significant upside potential for 2027 and 2028 estimates.

Furthermore, Pajjuri noted that Marvell's scale-across offering is emerging as an additional growth catalyst for 2027, while scale-up networking is expected to present a multibillion-dollar greenfield serviceable addressable market. Also, management is upbeat about Marvell's custom business, with the company targeting more than $10 billion in revenue for 2028, driven by existing programs with Amazon's AWS and Microsoft and multiple XPU attach wins.

Pajjuri ranks No. 88 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 51.5%. See Marvell Options Activity on TipRanks.

Chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is scheduled to announce its second-quarter earnings on Aug. 4. Shares have seen a strong jump year-to-date due to demand for the company's AI GPUs and server CPUs.

Ahead of second-quarter earnings, Wells Fargo analyst Aaron Rakers reaffirmed a buy rating on AMD stock and raised his price target to $615 from $505, citing "increasing focus on path to +$20/sh. EPS in CY28." The analyst expects AMD to reiterate its confidence in the MI450 series and Helios ramp beginning in the third quarter of 2026.

The 5-star analyst increased his estimates for AMD server CPU revenue to $16.0 billion (up 68% year-over-year), $20.5 billion (up 28%), and $25.0 billion (up 22%) for 2026, 2027, 2028, respectively. Rakers noted that in the previous quarter, AMD increased its server CPU total addressable market estimates to $120 billion by 2030, representing a more than 35% compound annual growth rate.

Rakers expects AMD to comment on an additional rise in server CPU demand since its first-quarter results. He sees upside driven by agentic AI demand momentum, cloud demand, and traditional enterprise modernization. In this regard, the analyst highlighted that Micron increased its 2026 server shipment guidance recently. Also, checks indicate continued upside to the average selling price.

Meanwhile, Rakers' data center GPU estimates remain above consensus at $15.6 billion, $40.6 billion, and $63.0 billion for 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively, while estimates for the client and gaming businesses are below the Street's consensus. Overall, the analyst projects EPS of $7.15, $13.40, and $18.75 for 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively.
